podcast.title: Day Job at Gallo Records
podcast.body: Linda secured a day job packing records for Gallo Records, the only record label in South Africa which also owned the only recording studio in Sub-Saharan Africa. This connection enabled him to get The Evening Birds signed. "It was because Solomon Linda got a day job packing records for Gallo records, the only record label in South Africa, which owned the only recording studio in Sub-Saharan Africa."

podcast.title: Death in Poverty
podcast.body: Solomon Linda died in 1962 with only 100 rand (equivalent to 50 British pounds then) in his bank account, and was buried in an unmarked grave. His song had become an international number one hit record a little over a year before his death, yet he saw none of the millions it earned for others. "When Linda died in 1962, he had a hundred grand, equivalent then to 50 British pounds, in his bank account."

podcast.title: Exploited for "In Boube" Success
podcast.body: Despite writing "In Boube," which sold 100,000 copies and gave its name to an entire music genre, Solomon Linda only earned ten shillings for it. This was estimated by the South African government to be a quarter of a week's poverty-level wages for a black family at the time. "It sold 100,000 copies on Gallo records, and earned Solomon Linda, its writer and lead singer, Ten Shillings."

podcast.title: Most Important South African Performer
podcast.body: In the 1930s and 1940s, Solomon Linda was probably the single most important performer in South Africa, leading the highly popular vocal group The Evening Birds. "Linda was, in the 30s and 40s, probably the single most important performer in South Africa."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Posthumous Royalty Battles for Family
podcast.body: Linda's family received only a couple of thousand dollars a year in royalties from the song for decades, while American copyright owners earned an estimated $15 million. Legal action in 2006 led to an out-of-court settlement with Disney and Aberlin Music, providing Linda's daughters with a lump sum and royalties until 2017, though most of the money went to legal bills. "The surviving sisters were told that the copyright in Inbube should have reverted to them in the 80s, and that they had a very good case under South African law to get a proper share of the rights to both Wimmerway and The Lion sleeps tonight."

podcast.title: Zulu Identity in Racist South Africa
podcast.body: Solomon Linda was a Zulu, which meant he was largely without rights in the racist regime of South Africa during the 1930s and 1940s. "Linda was a Zulu, and thus in the racist regime of South Africa was largely without rights."
